assignments.title: Science Graphic Organizer: Variables
assignments.html:
🧩 Science Graphic Organizer: Variables

Throughout the year, you’re going to see Science Graphic Organizers included in our weekly modules.

 

These are NOT graded assignments, and you do not have to submit them to Canvas. They are optional resources that I am giving you to help you organize what we’re learning and build your Science Notebook into something you can actually use throughout the year.

 

That being said...

⭐ I HIGHLY recommend using them! ⭐

 

Graphic organizers take a lot of the information we’re learning and put it into a visual format that is easier to understand, organize, and come back to later. They can be especially helpful when you’re studying for a quiz or test and need a quick reminder of something we learned several weeks ago.

 

For variables, this organizer is going to be especially useful as we work through our Science Fair projects. You will need to identify variables in your own experiment, so having a reference page in your Science Notebook can save you a LOT of confusion later!

 

Think of this as another tool in your science toolkit. 🧰🔬

🖨️ If You Want to Add It to Your Science Notebook...

I've included the Variables graphic organizer for this week's science content.

 

If you decide this resource would be helpful for you, you can:

  1. Print the graphic organizer included in this module.

  2. Color and complete it as we work through the week's science content.

  3. Use different colors to separate the different types of variables or make important ideas stand out.

  4. Add it to your Science Notebook using whatever organization system you've chosen.

 

If you're using a traditional notebook, you can glue or tape it onto a page.

If you're using a three-pronged folder, you can hole-punch it and add it with your other materials.

If you're using a binder, you can add it directly to your binder or slide it into a sheet protector.

 

Remember: your Science Notebook does not have to look exactly like anyone else's. Organize it in the way that works best for YOU.

🎨 Do I HAVE to Color It?

Nope.

Color coding can be really useful for this organizer because it can help you visually separate the independent variable, dependent variable, and controlled variables.

But this isn't an art contest. 😂

 

If coloring helps you learn, use it! If you'd rather highlight important vocabulary, add your own examples, write notes beside each type of variable, or simply keep the organizer as a reference page, that's completely fine too.

The goal is to make the resource useful to you.

⭐ Is This Graded?

NO! This graphic organizer is completely optional.

 

There are:

❌ No points
❌ No Canvas submission
❌ No required photo
❌ No grade for completing it

 

But don't confuse optional with not useful.

I HIGHLY recommend keeping this particular organizer in your Science Notebook, especially during our Science Fair quarter. When it's time to identify the variables in your own experiment, you'll already have a reference ready to go.

🧠 Why Should I Keep It?

Your Science Notebook isn't just a place to put assignments and then forget about them.

 

We're building a resource that you can continue adding to as we learn. By the end of the year, it should be filled with your Science Logs, diagrams, observations, notes, graphic organizers, reference materials, and all kinds of evidence of the science we've explored together. Variables aren't something we're going to learn once and never see again. You'll use them when you're planning experiments, collecting data, analyzing results, and working through your Science Fair project.

 

When it's time to identify the variables in your own experiment, I want you to be able to open your notebook and think:

“Oh! I remember this!”

 

So no, you don't have to add this graphic organizer to your notebook. But Science-Fair-you might be REALLY glad you did. 😉🔬

– Ms. Orlando 🦈

🔬 Variables: What Changes, What You Measure & What Stays the Same

When scientists design a controlled experiment, they need to know exactly what they are changing, what they are measuring, and what they are keeping the same.

🧪 Independent Variable — The factor the scientist intentionally changes during the experiment.

📊 Dependent Variable — The factor the scientist measures or observes to see what happened because of the change.

🔒 Controlled Variables — The factors that are kept the same so the experiment is a fair test.

 

Here's a quick way to think about it:

Independent = I CHANGE it
Dependent = I MEASURE it
Controls = I KEEP them the SAME

 

As you begin planning your Science Fair experiment, you'll need to be able to identify each of these.

Change ONE thing. Measure what happens. Keep everything else as consistent as possible. That's how we build a fair test! 🔬📊

💡 Reminder

Your science notebook is one of the most important tools you’ll use this year. Keeping it organized, neat, and colorful will make it easier for you to review before quizzes, tests, and projects. quizzes.title: Understanding Variables in Scientific Experiments: Quiz

questions.text: A scientist investigates how water temperature affects the amount of time it takes a tablet to dissolve. The scientist uses water at different temperatures and records the dissolving time. What is the independent variable?

answers.text: The amount of time the tablet takes to dissolve
The type of tablet being used
The method used to measure time

questions.text: A student investigates how the height of a ramp affects the distance a toy car travels. The student changes the ramp height and measures how far the car travels after leaving the ramp. What is the dependent variable?

answers.text: The distance the toy car travels
The surface used for the experiment

questions.text: A scientist wants to determine whether the amount of fertilizer affects tomato plant growth. Each group receives a different amount of fertilizer, but all plants receive the same amount of water and light and are grown for the same amount of time. Why are the water, light, and growing time kept the same?

answers.text: They are controlled variables that help make the comparison fair.
They are independent variables that the scientist is testing.
They are dependent variables that must be measured at the end.
They form the control group because they do not receive fertilizer.

questions.text: A student wants to test whether fertilizer affects plant growth. Plant A receives fertilizer, more water, and more sunlight. Plant B receives no fertilizer, less water, and less sunlight. Plant A grows taller. Why can the student NOT conclude that the fertilizer caused the increased growth?

answers.text: Plant height cannot be used as a dependent variable.
Plants cannot be used to investigate cause-and-effect relationships.
Every experiment must have more than one independent variable.
Several important factors changed, so it is unclear which change affected the plant's growth.

questions.text: A student is testing whether a new fertilizer affects plant growth. One group receives the fertilizer, while another group receives no fertilizer. Both groups receive the same type of soil, amount of water, and amount of sunlight. Which statement correctly distinguishes the control group from the controlled variables?

answers.text: The group receiving fertilizer is the control group, while plant growth is a controlled variable.
The group receiving no fertilizer can serve as the control group, while the soil, water, and sunlight are controlled variables.
The soil, water, and sunlight make up the control group, while the group receiving no fertilizer is the dependent variable.
The control group and controlled variables are two names for the same part of an experiment.

quizzes.description: Five multiple-choice questions based directly on the Weekly Reading. Complete the reading before attempting the quiz.

quizzes.title: Biotechnology: Changing Life Through Science: Quiz

questions.text: Which statement correctly compares cloning, genetic engineering, and artificial selection?

answers.text: Cloning directly changes DNA, genetic engineering produces identical copies, and artificial selection occurs without human involvement.
Cloning copies genetic information, genetic engineering directly changes genetic information, and artificial selection involves humans choosing organisms with desired traits to reproduce.
Cloning and genetic engineering are forms of artificial selection because all three require humans to choose which organisms reproduce.
Cloning, genetic engineering, and artificial selection all change DNA directly in a laboratory.

questions.text: A farmer repeatedly breeds plants that naturally produce larger fruits so that this characteristic becomes more common in future generations. Which biotechnology is the farmer using?

Scientists directly modify the DNA of a crop so that the plant has resistance to a particular insect pest. What is one reason scientists should ALSO study the environmental effects of this genetically engineered crop?

answers.text: The modified crop could interact with other organisms, and scientists need to investigate effects such as changes in insect populations or the movement of genes to related plants.
Any genetic modification will automatically damage every species living near the crop.
Genetically engineered plants cannot interact with other organisms once their DNA has been changed.
Environmental effects are important only when scientists clone an organism, not when they genetically engineer one.

questions.text: Scientists use genetically engineered microorganisms to help produce human insulin for medical use. Which choice BEST describes an impact of this biotechnology on an individual?

answers.text: It demonstrates that all genetically engineered organisms are clones.
It causes artificially selected traits to become more common in a population.
It guarantees that genetic engineering never creates risks or tradeoffs.
It can help provide a medication needed by people who require insulin as part of their medical treatment.

questions.text: Why is it important to consider both the benefits and possible risks or tradeoffs of biotechnology?

answers.text: Scientists can determine whether biotechnology is good or bad simply by identifying which process was used.
Biotechnology affects only individual organisms, so effects on society and the environment do not need to be considered.
A biotechnology can provide useful benefits while also creating risks or unintended consequences for individuals, society, or the environment.
A biotechnology should be considered harmful whenever it changes an organism or its genetic information.

quizzes.title: Fossils and Rock Layers: Quiz

questions.text: A seashell is pressed into soft mud. The mud hardens into stone, and the shell decays, leaving a hollow print in the rock. What type of fossil is the hollow print?
Minerals fill in the hollow print of a clam shell and leave a 3D stone copy of the shell. What type of fossil is the stone copy?
A mammoth is found frozen in ice, with its actual body preserved. What type of fossil is it?

answers.text: Trace fossil, because it shows how the mammoth lived
Mold fossil, because the ice holds its shape
True form fossil, because it preserves the actual organism
Cast fossil, because minerals filled its body

questions.text: In which kind of rock layers are fossils most often found?

answers.text: Sedimentary rock layers, formed when mud, sand, and minerals are packed together and hardened
Rock layers made only of hardened tree sap
Layers of ice at the poles
Fossils are found equally in every kind of rock

questions.text: A scientist studies undisturbed rock layers. According to the Law of Superposition, where would the oldest fossils be?

answers.text: There is no way to tell which fossils are older

quizzes.description: Five multiple-choice questions based directly on the Weekly Reading and the Fossils & Rock Layers Quick Reference Guide. Complete the reading before attempting the quiz.

quizzes.title: Our Solar System: Quiz

questions.text: Earth is often called the "Goldilocks Planet." Counting outward from the Sun, which planet is Earth?
What keeps all the planets, moons, and asteroids in orbit around the Sun?
Which layer of Earth is a liquid layer of molten metal that generates Earth's magnetic field?
What causes day and night on Earth?

answers.text: Earth's rotation: it spins once every 24 hours
Earth's revolution: it orbits the Sun every 365 days
The Sun turning off and on

questions.text: What is the habitable zone?

answers.text: The part of Earth where people live
The distance from a star where liquid water can exist
The asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter
The layer of gases around Earth

quizzes.description: Five multiple-choice questions based directly on the Weekly Reading and the Our Solar System Quick Reference Guide. Complete the reading before attempting the quiz.

quizzes.title: Layers of the Earth: Quiz

questions.text: Convection currents in the mantle move Earth's plates. What happens to the rock in mantle convection?

answers.text: Hot rock rises and cool rock sinks
Cool rock rises and hot rock sinks
The rock melts into liquid metal

questions.text: Which is Earth's thickest layer, at about 2,900 km?
Where does Earth's magnetic field come from?

answers.text: The movement of the liquid outer core

questions.text: The lithosphere includes continental crust and oceanic crust. Which describes continental crust?
According to the guide, what would happen without Earth's magnetic field?

answers.text: Solar wind would strip away Earth's atmosphere

quizzes.description: Five multiple-choice questions based directly on the Weekly Reading and the Layers of the Earth Quick Reference Guide. Complete the reading before attempting the quiz.

quizzes.title: Quarter 2 Final

questions.text: Which layer of Earth is the only liquid layer?
The inner core is the hottest layer of Earth. Why is it solid?

answers.text: The pressure is so high that the metals cannot melt
It is made of cool rock
It is the farthest layer from the Sun
It is colder than the crust

questions.text: What is the mantle made of?

answers.text: Hot, solid silicate rock that flows very slowly
Gases held in place by gravity

questions.text: What are the outer core and the inner core both made of?
Scientists cannot dig to the center of Earth. What do they use to learn which layers are solid or liquid?

answers.text: Samples dug from the inner core

questions.text: What do convection currents in the mantle do?

answers.text: Move the tectonic plates on top of the mantle

questions.text: What does the hydrosphere include?

answers.text: All of Earth's water, whether it is solid, liquid, or gas
The layer of gases around Earth

questions.text: Which gas makes up most of Earth's atmosphere?
In which layer of the atmosphere does weather happen?
What does the ozone layer do?
Where is most of Earth's freshwater stored?
What is erosion?

answers.text: Hot rock rising in the mantle

questions.text: Hurricanes are an example of which two spheres interacting?

answers.text: The atmosphere and the hydrosphere: hurricanes form over warm ocean water
The lithosphere and the inner core
The mantle and the outer core

questions.text: A volcano erupts and sends ash high into the air. Which spheres are interacting?

answers.text: The hydrosphere and the inner core
The atmosphere and the outer core

questions.text: Where do earthquakes occur?

answers.text: Only in the middle of oceans
Only at the North and South Poles

questions.text: A river carves a deep valley over time. Which sphere is shaping which?

answers.text: The hydrosphere is shaping the lithosphere
The atmosphere is shaping the hydrosphere
The lithosphere is shaping the atmosphere
The inner core is shaping the hydrosphere

questions.text: Which shows the four steps of natural selection in order?

answers.text: Variation, environmental change, survival and reproduction, adaptation over time
Adaptation over time, variation, survival and reproduction, environmental change
Environmental change, adaptation over time, variation, survival and reproduction
Survival and reproduction, variation, adaptation over time, environmental change

questions.text: A giraffe's long neck helps it reach tall leaves. What type of adaptation is it?
A camel stores water inside its body. What type of adaptation is this?
Humans breed dogs for certain traits. What is this called?
What is the main process that drives evolution?
"How does the amount of water affect plant height?" What is the independent variable?
What should a good hypothesis connect?

answers.text: The independent variable to the dependent variable
The control group to the weather

questions.text: In a fair experiment, how many independent variables should a scientist change at a time?
What is a control group?

answers.text: A comparison group that does not receive the treatment being tested
The conditions kept the same throughout an experiment
The variable the scientist changes on purpose
